query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The accelerated coupled degradation of a multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature arises from tribo‐mechanical removal of its high‐temperature passive oxide film at lamellar phase boundaries, exposing anodic eutectic phases to localized microgalvanic attack; corrosion undermines the mechanical integrity at phase interfaces and promotes further wear, leading to a synergistic mass loss exceeding the sum of individual wear and corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Cast multi-phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy with lamellar α/β phases, dewetted high-temperature oxide passivation film, average grain size ~5 μm, no prior mechanical polishing.
generation.intervention: Sliding wear under a 10 N normal load at 300 °C in 3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous vapor for 10^4 cycles, with simultaneous electrochemical control at open‐circuit potential.
generation.conditions: Temperature: 300 ± 10 °C; sliding speed: 15 cm/s; normal load: 10 N; environment: 3.5 wt% NaCl vapor with O2 partial pressure ≥0.1 atm; cycle count: 10 000; pH ~6.
generation.structural_mediator: Integrity and regrowth kinetics of the high‐temperature passive oxide film at α/β phase boundaries and the galvanic potential difference between eutectic phases.
generation.mechanism: Mechanical wear repeatedly strips the protective oxide, exposing fresh α/β interfaces that act as microanodes; rapid localized corrosion (pitting) occurs at these sites, embrittling the material and increasing material removal by wear; corrosion defects concentrate stress and accelerate oxide breakdown.
generation.predicted_outcome: 1) Total mass loss under combined wear+corrosion > (mass loss_wear-only + mass loss_corrosion-only). 2) Wear mass loss in combined test > wear-only by a noticeable margin. 3) Corrosion current (I_corr) in combined test > I_corr in static corrosion-only by a noticeable margin.
generation.baseline: Homogenized single-phase equiatomic high-entropy alloy (same overall composition) with no lamellar eutectic microstructure, tested under identical wear+corrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: Valid for chloride concentration 1–5 wt% NaCl, temperature 250–350 °C, sliding speeds 10–20 cm/s, normal loads 5–15 N, oxygen partial pressure ≥0.05 atm, cycle counts up to 10^5; outside these ranges mechanisms may differ.
generation.uncertainty: Moderate; while the direction of synergistic mass loss is well supported by general tribocorrosion principles, the precise magnitudes of wear and corrosion enhancement are not quantified without direct experiment.

falsification_experiment.design: Three factorial tests on the eutectic alloy: (A) wear-only in inert Ar at 300 °C; (B) static corrosion-only immersion in 3.5 wt% NaCl at 300 °C; (C) combined wear+corrosion under identical mechanical and environmental parameters. Include parallel tests on the homogenized single-phase baseline.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If (mass loss_C ≤ mass loss_A + mass loss_B) AND (wear_C ≈ wear_A) AND (I_corr_C ≤ I_corr_B), or if corrosion attack is uniformly distributed rather than localized at phase boundaries, then the hypothesis is falsified.
